mechanism: Each offer is written as one scoped outcome with a name the buyer already uses (missed-call text-back, review requests, dormant-customer reactivation) instead of a general AI service. why_not_testable: Testing it means putting offers in front of real buyers, which needs outreach and an audience.

one_line: Selling one named job, like missed-call text-back, instead of 'AI', gives the buyer a single number to judge you on.
idea_why: A single measurable outcome per offer is an old and well-understood sales mechanism, and it fits automations that are small and checkable.
breakdown: Pick three jobs with an obvious counter (missed calls, review requests, lapsed customers). For each, write a one-sentence promise, a before and after metric, and a minimal automation that produces the metric. Build the automation with Claude Code and a webhook or SMS API, log every event to a CSV so the number is real. Then put each offer in front of a small list of one trade type. A hired person would do the calling and onboarding that no script covers.

mechanism: A general Codex-based agent is run unchanged across ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze and Terminal-Bench, with only one instruction varied: report difficulties and return control for automatic continuation. That alone raises mean scores on two benchmarks. Moving the reset decision into a scripted controller that follows a convention already given to the agent recovers part of the gap to a specialised agent. Gains cost more tokens, and the paper says it cannot separate better use from extra inference.
claim: A one-line instruction change and a scripted reset controller improve a general agent, but it still trails an ARC-AGI-3-specific agent.
why_not_testable: Needs a Codex-class agent and benchmark environments with model calls.

one_line: Moving the 'when to reset' decision out of the model and into a plain script recovered some of a specialist agent's lead.
idea_why: Handing control decisions to deterministic code while keeping the model for content is a plausible and cheap scaffolding change.
breakdown: Take any agent loop, find the decisions that follow a fixed rule (reset, retry, stop), and move them into a controller script. Keep the same prompt otherwise and compare scores plus token cost on a fixed task set. Report cost alongside score because the paper warns they move together.

mechanism: A pump.fun launch mints one billion tokens and places 800 million on a bonding curve, so price rises with the amount bought. The speaker reports roughly 85 to 86 SOL fills the curve and sends it to Raydium, with King of the Hill at about 45 SOL. He reconstructs the curve by interpolating from buy transactions (SOL in, tokens out), because he did not know the formula. The formula is likely a constant-product style virtual reserve curve that can be read from the program account.
claim: About 86 SOL fills the curve and about 45 SOL reaches King of the Hill, with price rising exponentially.
verdict_question: Does a live pump.fun bonding curve account read from public Solana RPC satisfy constant product on its virtual reserves, and does it graduate at about 85 SOL of real reserves?
probe_title: pump.fun curve: does a live curve account obey constant product and graduate near 85 SOL real reserves?
one_line: Pump.fun's curve holds 800 million of a billion tokens and fills at about 86 SOL; I will read a live curve account and check the maths.
idea_why: A bonding curve is a deterministic formula, so claims about its fill cost can be checked against on-chain reserves.
breakdown: Fetch a recent token's bonding-curve account from a public Solana RPC, decode virtual and real reserves, and compute k. Check price after a buy against the formula and compare real SOL reserves at graduation with the 85 to 86 SOL claim. The result feeds the Grinder's entry-price and slippage model directly.

mechanism: Instead of budgets, each income and spending category is projected forward from its own history and placed in the account where it usually lands (paycheques and rent in checking, daily spending on cards). Card payments are modelled from the projected card balance, so cash leaves checking when the bill is due, not when the charge is made. User-defined recurring transfers model savings. The output is a forecast of cash balance over time.
claim: A cash flow projection engine that models credit card timing, replacing monthly budgets.
why_not_testable: Needs real transaction data, which Proteus has none of and should not request.
one_line: A finance app forecasts cash by modelling when card bills actually leave the bank, not when you spend.
idea_why: Separating the charge date from the cash date is the correct fix for the common net-of-the-month cash flow error.
breakdown: Take a transactions CSV, assign each category to its usual account, project each category with a trailing average and day-of-month pattern, then model card payments as the prior statement balance paid on the due date. Plot the running balance and back-test by forecasting a held-out month. The same projection logic could suit any recurring cash flow.

mechanism: A Tessendorf FFT ocean runs as WebGPU compute shaders: six 256 by 256 cascades from 1103 m down to 0.26 m patches, driven by a JONSWAP wind spectrum with directional spreading and swell. The mesh is a 17-level CDLOD quadtree and shading uses LEAN-mapped slope moments for roughness at distance, with foam from the surface Jacobian folding. The whole thing bundles into one 61 KB minified HTML file.
claim: A from-scratch WebGPU ocean renderer in a single 61 KB HTML file, built with Claude Code.
verdict_question: Does ocean.min.html download at about 61 KB and load in the Browser pane with a WebGPU adapter and no console errors?

breakdown: Fetch the minified HTML from the repo, check its byte size, then open it in a browser with WebGPU enabled and read the console. Take a screenshot to confirm a sea is drawn. The wave and shading techniques are reusable for any HyperFrames or still-render background.

mechanism: PROBE trains an LLM auditor to talk to a deployed tool-using agent as a realistic user across several turns and trigger policy violations (pricing, privacy, confirmation). It treats the exchange as a two-player Markov game with a composite reward balancing violation discovery, plausibility, progress and policy diversity. GRPO, DPO and GFlowNet objectives are compared. Trained auditors find broader violations than same-size zero-shot adversaries, even against larger targets.
claim: Trained multi-turn auditors uncover broader policy violations in tool-using agents than zero-shot adversaries.
why_not_testable: Needs model training or at least model calls, and no local LLM exists here.
needs: Model access and a target agent.
one_line: Auditors trained on a reward for plausible, diverse violations find more rule-breaking in agents than untrained attackers.
idea_why: Multi-turn probing with a diversity reward addresses violations that single-prompt red-teaming cannot reach.
breakdown: Write the policy as a list of checkable rules, give an auditor model a user persona and the agent's tool log, and reward turns that cause a logged violation while staying plausible. Without training, a simple version is a scripted set of personas run against the agent and a rule checker over the tool log. That would suit testing Proteus's own hook.
